===== WORLD 13 · LESSON range_advantage · Range advantage =====

TASK w13_1_teach [theory] What should you compare first when reading range advantage?
CAPTION: Study range advantage.
TEACH: What should you compare first when reading range advantage? Range advantage compares two sets of possible hands on the same board. Start with each range’s surviving combinations. Compare the share that reaches a named strength or use a full equity calculation. The strongest single hand is a separate question.
Q: What should you compare first when reading range advantage?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The share of qualifying combinations — Correct. Reading the share shows how often each range hits the board. It is more informative than one possible monster.
  - [wrong] The strongest hand either player can hold — Look again. That identifies the nuts, but it does not tell you how common the other strong hands are.
    BETTER ANSWER: The share of qualifying combinations
  - [wrong] Who made the last bet — Look again. The last bet tells you who took the lead. The board and surviving combinations determine which range connects more often.
    BETTER ANSWER: The share of qualifying combinations

===== WORLD 13 · LESSON nut_advantage · Nut advantage =====

TASK w13_2_teach [theory] What would show that one range has the strongest hand more often?
CAPTION: Study nut advantage.
TEACH: What would show that one range has the strongest hand more often? The nuts are the strongest possible hand on the current board. A nut advantage means that hand occurs more often in one range. Card removal means excluding combinations containing visible cards. The range with more overpairs may still have fewer nuts on a flop with consecutive ranks.
Q: What would show that one range has the strongest hand more often?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] A larger share of the strongest possible hand — Correct. Count the strongest legal hand inside each range. That reveals a nut edge even when the other player has more overpairs.
  - [wrong] More overpairs after card removal — Look again. An overpair is behind a straight when the board supports one. Count the strongest possible hands separately.
    BETTER ANSWER: A larger share of the strongest possible hand
  - [wrong] Being the preflop raiser — Look again. The raiser can represent strength. The caller may actually hold the strongest hand more often.
    BETTER ANSWER: A larger share of the strongest possible hand

===== WORLD 13 · LESSON equity_vs_range · Equity vs range =====

TASK w13_3_teach [theory] Which method estimates equity against an explicit range?
CAPTION: Study your equity against possible hands.
TEACH: Which method estimates equity against an explicit range? Equity is your average share at showdown. Expand the opponent’s range into legal combinations, remove known cards and count each win as one and each two-player tie as half. You price a call with the final pot after calling.
Q: Which method estimates equity against an explicit range?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] Average wins and half of ties over legal combos and runouts — Correct. Each legal combination and runout contributes to the average. Half of each tie counts the share you take at showdown.
  - [wrong] Pick one hand that looks typical — Look again. One hand hides how often stronger and weaker combinations occur. Enumerate the whole stated range.
    BETTER ANSWER: Average wins and half of ties over legal combos and runouts
  - [wrong] Give each shorthand hand family equal weight — Look again. A suited hand and a pocket pair contribute different numbers of combinations. Count combinations after removing visible cards.
    BETTER ANSWER: Average wins and half of ties over legal combos and runouts

TASK w13_3_read_same_hand_two_ranges [drill] Against which range does your A-J have more equity?
CAPTION: Compare two equally weighted BB ranges after removing visible cards. Range A is AJs AQo AKo 88. Range B is A9s ATo KQs 76s 99. No betting or folding assumptions are needed for showdown equity.
Q: Against which range does your A-J have more equity?

  - [wrong] Range A — Look again. A-Q, A-K and a set of eights leave A-J behind too often. The equal A-J combinations do not make Range A easier.
    BETTER ANSWER: Range B

    FEEDBACK TABLE: Flop | You Ah Jd | Board Ad 8s 5c | Pot 5.5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Card focus board_0, board_1, board_2 | Facts one pair, top pair, rainbow

===== WORLD 13 · LESSON equity_realization · Equity realization =====

TASK w13_4_teach [theory] What can make the same showdown equity worth less in a played hand?
CAPTION: Study equity realization.
TEACH: What can make the same showdown equity worth less in a played hand? Showdown equity assumes you get to see the last card. Equity realization means the share you actually turn into chips after future bets and folds. In position, a check behind can close a street. Stack depth changes the bets still possible.
Q: What can make the same showdown equity worth less in a played hand?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] A later bet that forces you to fold some potential wins — Correct. A later bet can end your hand before showdown. Those surrendered wins reduce the amount you can realize.
  - [wrong] Moving seats changes the raw equity of identical cards and ranges — Look again. Holding cards, board and ranges fixed holds showdown equity fixed. Position changes the betting choices you face.
    BETTER ANSWER: A later bet that forces you to fold some potential wins
  - [wrong] The full equity share is paid out on the turn — Look again. Chips are awarded at showdown or when everyone else folds. A turn equity number is not a payout.
    BETTER ANSWER: A later bet that forces you to fold some potential wins

===== WORLD 13 · LESSON backdoor_draws · Backdoor draws =====

TASK w13_5_teach [theory] Two remaining cards
CAPTION: Study backdoor draws.
TEACH: Two remaining cards A backdoor flush draw is a draw that needs a card of the right suit on both the turn and river. With exactly three cards of one suit across your hand and the flop, both remaining cards must be of that suit. A backdoor straight also needs both cards. With 7-6 on A-9-2, an 8 plus either a 5 or a ten completes it. Completing either draw is different from winning the pot.
Q: What is true of a backdoor flush draw on the flop?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] Both remaining cards must be of the suit — Correct. You have three cards of that suit available. A flush needs five, so the turn and river must both add one.
  - [wrong] A single card of the suit completes it — Look again. One card gives you only four of the suit. A direct flush draw already has four on the flop.
    BETTER ANSWER: Both remaining cards must be of the suit
  - [wrong] Completing it guarantees you win — Look again. A higher flush or a full house may still win. Completion probability is only one part of equity.
    BETTER ANSWER: Both remaining cards must be of the suit

===== WORLD 13 · LESSON initiative_cbet_checkpoint · Initiative cbet checkpoint =====

TASK w13_6_teach [theory] What should decide whether you follow your earlier raise with a c-bet?
CAPTION: Study initiative cbet checkpoint.
TEACH: What should decide whether you follow your earlier raise with a c-bet? The last aggressive action gives a player the initiative, which is an opportunity to represent a range. A c-bet is a flop bet by the preflop aggressor. A check-raise can take over aggression. Before betting, ask what worse hands call or what better hands fold.
Q: What should decide whether you follow your earlier raise with a c-bet?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The board and how the other range reacts — Correct. A c-bet works when the opposing range gives it a purpose. The board and likely calls or folds matter more than having raised first.
  - [wrong] The preflop raise obliges the raiser to c-bet — Look again. A check can protect your showdown share when betting only keeps strong hands in. Initiative does not force a bet.
    BETTER ANSWER: The board and how the other range reacts
  - [wrong] Acting last gives a player the initiative — Look again. Position determines who acts last. Aggression determines initiative, so the two can belong to different seats.
    BETTER ANSWER: The board and how the other range reacts

TASK w13_6_read_check_raise_transfer [drill] Who has taken over the aggression on this flop?
CAPTION: BTN opened before the flop. Compare who acts next with who made the latest aggressive action.
Q: Who has taken over the aggression on this flop?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Flop | You Qh Tc | Board 9d 7s 3c | Pot 14.5 BB | To call 5 BB | Seat BTN | Active btn | Decision btn | Facts high card, rainbow, backdoor straight

TRAIL: preflop: SB posts 0.5 BB · preflop: BB posts 1 BB · preflop: UTG folds · preflop: HJ folds · preflop: CO folds · preflop: BTN raises to 2.5 BB · preflop: SB folds · preflop: BB calls 1.5 BB more · flop: BB checks · flop: BTN bets 2 BB · flop: BB raises to 7 BB
  + [correct] BB, after the check-raise — Correct. BB’s raise is the latest aggressive action. BTN now faces a decision, but being next to act does not restore initiative.
  - [wrong] BTN, because BTN opened preflop — Look again. BTN had the preflop initiative. BB’s later raise took over the aggression on this street.
    BETTER ANSWER: BB, after the check-raise
  - [wrong] Neither player, because BB first checked — Look again. The flop check preceded the raise. Use the latest aggressive action rather than the first action.
    BETTER ANSWER: BB, after the check-raise

===== WORLD 14 · LESSON merged_underbet · Merged underbet =====

TASK w14_1_teach [theory] When does a small bet with strong and medium-strength hands earn value?
CAPTION: Study merged underbet.
TEACH: When does a small bet with strong and medium-strength hands earn value? A merged bet is a bet with strong and medium-strength hands that can get paid by worse. A below-pot bet is an underbet. Small sizes can keep more of the opponent’s range in when that opponent calls with weaker made hands.
Q: When does a small bet with strong and medium-strength hands earn value?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] When more worse made hands will pay — Correct. A smaller bet can get calls from weaker pairs that fold to a larger size. Estimate those calls before choosing the amount.
  - [wrong] Whenever you have a medium-strength hand — Look again. A medium-strength hand may earn more by checking if betting keeps only stronger hands in the pot.
    BETTER ANSWER: When more worse made hands will pay
  - [wrong] When sets and bluffs form the betting range — Look again. Sets and bluffs describe a polarized selection. A merged range also bets some hands between those ends.
    BETTER ANSWER: When more worse made hands will pay

===== WORLD 14 · LESSON polarized_sizing · Polarized sizing =====

TASK w14_2_teach [theory] Which group is polarized?
CAPTION: Study polarized sizing.
TEACH: Which group is polarized? Strong value means hands that can bet profitably for calls from worse hands. A polarized betting range uses very strong value hands and bluffs, with many medium-strength hands checking. A larger size can support that split. Size alone cannot tell you whether any specific bet is value or a bluff.
Q: Which group is polarized?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] Strong value and bluffs with middle hands mostly checking — Correct. The strongest hands want calls and bluffs want folds. Many middle hands preserve value by checking in this strategy.
  - [wrong] Strong and medium made hands that aim to get paid — Look again. That is a merged value selection. It lacks the split between the strongest and weakest hands.
    BETTER ANSWER: Strong value and bluffs with middle hands mostly checking
  - [wrong] Mostly medium-strength hands sized up together — Look again. Medium hands are not the two ends of a range. Choosing a big amount does not make those hands polarized.
    BETTER ANSWER: Strong value and bluffs with middle hands mostly checking

===== WORLD 14 · LESSON read_sizing_and_abstraction · Read sizing and abstraction =====

TASK w14_3_teach [theory] What justifies using two sizes instead of one in a stated model?
CAPTION: Study read sizing and abstraction.
TEACH: What justifies using two sizes instead of one in a stated model? A size is a range clue only when you know something about the player’s use of that size. A single-size strategy is a deliberate simplification. Multiple sizes can give different ranges a better tool at the cost of more decisions.
Q: What justifies using two sizes instead of one in a stated model?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The two sizes serve different classes and improve average EV — Correct. Choose distinct sizes when they improve payoffs for different hands. A single size can still be a reasonable simplification.
  - [wrong] Adding a second size itself increases profitability — Look again. If the responses and payoffs are the same, an extra size adds a decision without a gain.
    BETTER ANSWER: The two sizes serve different classes and improve average EV
  - [wrong] The biggest size tells you a specific opponent hand — Look again. A size may change the likely types of hands. It does not expose an exact holding.
    BETTER ANSWER: The two sizes serve different classes and improve average EV

===== WORLD 14 · LESSON spr_and_commitment · Spr and commitment =====

TASK w14_4_teach [theory] What is enough to decide a low-SPR all-in call?
CAPTION: Study spr and commitment.
TEACH: What is enough to decide a low-SPR all-in call? SPR compares the shorter remaining stack with the street-start pot. A low SPR limits later bets. It does not make every top pair a call. For an all-in, compare your equity against the shoving range (the hands the opponent would bet all-in with) with the equity required to call.
Q: What is enough to decide a low-SPR all-in call?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] The actual call price and equity against the shoving range — Correct. A shorter stack can change the price and the result. Compare your equity against the opponent’s all-in hands with the equity required to call.
  - [wrong] Low SPR and top pair alone — Look again. Top pair can have too little equity against a strong range, even when the SPR is low.
    BETTER ANSWER: The actual call price and equity against the shoving range
  - [wrong] The players’ starting stacks before preflop — Look again. Preflop chips already invested are in the pot. Use the smaller amount remaining at the start of this street.
    BETTER ANSWER: The actual call price and equity against the shoving range

===== WORLD 14 · LESSON pot_geometry · Pot geometry =====

TASK w14_5_teach [theory] What makes the chip size rise under a constant pot fraction?
CAPTION: Study pot geometry.
TEACH: What makes the chip size rise under a constant pot fraction? Plan the river size before betting earlier streets. A called bet adds twice its amount to the pot and subtracts its amount from each remaining stack. Geometric sizing aims for similar fractions of the updated pot, rather than equal chip amounts.
Q: What makes the chip size rise under a constant pot fraction?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] Each call increases the pot used for the next size — Correct. Your bet and the call go into the pot. The same fraction therefore represents more chips on the next street.
  - [wrong] The bet enters the pot but the call does not — Look again. A matched call adds the same amount as the bet. Count both contributions.
    BETTER ANSWER: Each call increases the pot used for the next size
  - [wrong] The fraction is applied again to the original pot — Look again. The plan uses the updated pot. Reusing the opening pot would repeat the chip amount.
    BETTER ANSWER: Each call increases the pot used for the next size

===== WORLD 14 · LESSON induce_and_checkpoint · Induce and checkpoint =====

TASK w14_6_teach [theory] What should you check before betting small to invite a raise?
CAPTION: Study induce and checkpoint.
TEACH: What should you check before betting small to invite a raise? A small bet can induce a raise when a player responds aggressively to that size. Plan how to respond before making the bet. Some raise ranges are strong enough to fold to, and others contain enough bluffs to call.
Q: What should you check before betting small to invite a raise?
HINT [hidden]: (none)
TABLE: Facts no applicable hand facts
  + [correct] Which hands raise and whether your response pays — Correct. A raise is helpful only if the extra calls or bluffs make money after you price your response. Compare that with checking or betting larger.
  - [wrong] Whether the bet is below half the pot — Look again. A small amount alone tells you little about how a particular opponent raises. Use the stated response.
    BETTER ANSWER: Which hands raise and whether your response pays
  - [wrong] Whether one past raise was a bluff — Look again. One observed result does not supply the relative shares of value hands and bluffs in the current range.
    BETTER ANSWER: Which hands raise and whether your response pays
